definition: Apprehensive means anxious or uneasy that something bad may be coming — gripped in advance by dread of a specific event ahead.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word apprehensive. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know apprehensive should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: She grew apprehensive as the interview panel fell silent and slowly passed her portfolio down the table.
Uneasy is weaker than apprehensive: an uneasy feeling is a vague flicker of discomfort that may have no clear cause, while apprehension grips harder — a named dread fixed on something specific ahead.
Panicked is stronger than apprehensive: an apprehensive person still thinks and functions while the dread builds, but panic overwhelms thought entirely, scattering it just when it is needed most.

Anxious means troubled by worry, and the worry can be broad or free-floating — you can feel anxious about everything and nothing. Apprehensive points its dread at a target: an apprehensive person is uneasy about a specific event coming toward them — a test, a verdict, a flight.

Wary means alert to possible danger and keeping your guard up — wariness lives in watchful behavior, in the double-check and the careful step. Apprehensive names the inner dread itself: you can act wary while feeling calm, but you cannot be apprehensive without the knot of fear about what may come.

The morning of her first solo flight, Dana ran the preflight checklist twice, then a third time.
The instructor had signed her off; the weather was perfect; nothing was wrong.
Still, taxiing to the runway alone, she caught herself rehearsing engine-failure procedures for a plane that hummed flawlessly, her mind seizing on every way the next forty minutes could go wrong.
She was not in danger — she was apprehensive.
Nothing bad has happened, and nothing may: Dana's fear is aimed entirely at what lies ahead, her thoughts gripped in advance by imagined trouble.
That forward-looking dread of a specific coming event is exactly what apprehensive describes.

And note the trap inside its own family: apprehend now usually means to arrest, but apprehensive keeps the older mental grasp — the mind closing around a feared tomorrow.

The morning of her first solo flight, Dana ran the checklist twice and then sat very still on the bench outside the hangar.
Her instructor recognized the mood.
Students on solo day are rarely afraid of flying itself; they are apprehensive about one moment in particular — the first landing with nobody in the right seat.
Dana could name the exact fear: flaring too high, ballooning, and having to go around while the whole flight school watched.
The dread did not stop her.
She taxied out, flew three circuits, and set the plane down gently each time.
Walking back, she admitted the knot in her stomach had been there all week — tied, she said, to a single date on the calendar.
